metadata.title: Own Salesforce For AI? Oracle's Order Book Demands A Look

content.text:
For the same bet on enterprise software, Oracle presents a clearer forward path backed by a massive backlog, while Salesforce asks investors to underwrite a future turnaround.
If you own Salesforce (CRM) or Oracle (ORCL), you are making the same fundamental bet: that businesses will keep spending heavily on software to run their operations, increasingly supercharged by artificial intelligence. They are two of the most direct ways to get exposure to this demand. Yet a sharp divergence in their forward-looking signals suggests one is on a much clearer path from here.
While both companies recently raised their guidance, the difference in scale is telling. One is booking massive, multi-year deals that provide years of visibility. The other is showing enormous user engagement with its new AI tools, but is asking investors to wait for a broad revenue reacceleration. For an investor choosing where to place their capital today, the decision hinges on that difference.
The Clearest Signal: A Tale of Two Forecasts
The cleanest signal of a company's future is its own forecast. At their latest reports, both Salesforce and Oracle raised their outlooks. But Oracle's was an order of magnitude larger. The company boosted its Q1 revenue growth guidance by nine percentage points, now expecting to grow around 28%. It expects its cloud revenue to grow a staggering 60%, a fourteen-point raise from its prior outlook. For the full fiscal year, it anticipates total revenue growth of 34%.
Salesforce also raised its guidance, but by a fraction of a percent for revenue and earnings. Management said it expects "organic revenue reacceleration in the second half of FY 27," but this is a projection, not a current reality reflected in its overall forecast. This contrast in confidence is the most important forward-looking data point an investor has right now.
Why Oracle's Outlook Is So Confident
Oracle's confidence is grounded in its order book. The company announced it signed "$67 billion in AI infrastructure contracts this quarter" alone. Its total remaining performance obligations (RPO), a measure of contracted future revenue, now stands at an immense $638 billion, up 363%. This figure represents a multi-year backlog of locked-in demand from customers building out their AI capabilities on Oracle's infrastructure.
This backlog is Oracle's moat. The company's advantage is its ability to "deliver the applications, the data, the infrastructure, the AI tooling, and the industry expertise together," as its management stated. Instead of merely renting servers, customers are building on a full stack where their most valuable asset, their own data, often already resides in an Oracle database. This creates high switching costs and a durable competitive edge.
Salesforce's Bet: From AI Usage to Revenue
Salesforce's forward case is built on adoption and potential. The company's AI tools are seeing massive use, having "processed 28.6 trillion tokens, up 152% quarter over quarter." Its Agentforce product line is now a business with over $1 billion in annual recurring revenue. The bull case is that this explosive usage is a powerful leading indicator. As evidence, management noted its top AI customers have increased their total Salesforce spend by 1.5x in the last year.
The challenge, however, is translating that enthusiasm into broad financial momentum. As one analyst noted on the company's call, key metrics like bookings have been "lagging a little bit," and core products like Tableau have seen softness. The story requires investors to believe that today's token consumption will become tomorrow's accelerated revenue, even though the wider financial indicators have yet to confirm it.
The Tradeoff: Contracted Visibility vs. Future Potential
The decision between these two stocks turns on one forward dimension: contracted visibility versus hoped-for conversion. Oracle offers a direct play on the AI infrastructure build-out, backed by a historic backlog. But this path carries significant risk. The company plans a net cash outlay of around $70 billion for capital expenditures in fiscal 2027 and will need to raise $40 billion in new capital to fund it, while warning that its "gross margin will step down" in the near term. We have explored the execution risk in Oracle's strategy before.
Salesforce offers a bet on the power of its platform and customer relationships. The risk is that the conversion of AI usage into revenue is slower or smaller than hoped, and you are paying a slightly richer valuation for a company with slower current growth while you wait. Its cleaner balance sheet provides a cushion, but the core bet is on a turnaround that has been promised but not yet delivered.
Prefer To Run The Numbers Your Own Way?
You can line Salesforce and Oracle up directly on the Salesforce peer comparison, weigh them on valuation, growth, margins, and returns, and swap in any other Application Software names you hold.
Asking that question of one pair is easy. Asking it of every stock you own, and re-asking it each quarter as the numbers move, is the part almost nobody keeps up with, and it is exactly where most portfolios quietly fall behind the market.
